Patient Vignette: Mr. R.

Mr. R. is a 54-year-old married Latin American man who owns a successful regional logistics company. He presents for therapy at the urging of his wife, who has noticed him becoming “a different person” over the past three years. He is a tall, solidly built man with graying hair and a direct, careful gaze. He speaks in a measured, low voice, as if choosing each word with great care.

He begins the first session by describing his work. For twenty years, he volunteered as a logistics coordinator for a non-governmental organization, organizing supply convoys into conflict zones. He was proud of this work—it felt like a duty. In 2021, during a deployment to a war-torn region, his convoy was ambushed. He describes the moment with a flat, almost mechanical precision: the sudden crack of gunfire, the smell of diesel and dust, the sight of his driver, a young man named Elias, taking a bullet to the chest. Mr. R. was pinned under the overturned truck for two hours, listening to the radio chatter of the attackers and the slow, wet breathing of Elias, who died beside him.

He was rescued, but the world has not felt the same since.

In the months after, Mr. R. threw himself back into his business. He worked eighteen-hour days, believing that if he just kept moving, the memory would fade. It did not. He now avoids all news about the region. His wife recently suggested a documentary about humanitarian work, and he left the room without a word, his hands shaking. He cannot drive past a military checkpoint without his heart pounding so hard he has to pull over. The sound of a helicopter overhead—common in his city for medical evacuations—sends him into a cold sweat.

At night, he does not sleep. He lies rigid in bed, listening for sounds that are not there. When he does drift off, he dreams of Elias’s face, the blood spreading across his shirt, the radio crackling with a language he cannot understand. He wakes gasping, his wife’s hand on his arm, and he does not tell her what he saw. He feels a profound, unshakeable guilt: he was the leader, the one who planned the route. He should have known. He replays the route in his head, over and over, looking for the mistake.

His business has suffered. He has become irritable with employees, snapping at small errors. He cancelled a major contract last month because the client’s office was in a building with a similar layout to the ambush site. He tells me he feels “numb” during family dinners, watching his children laugh, but feeling as if he is watching them through a thick pane of glass. He has stopped attending his church, a place that once gave him deep comfort, because the smell of incense reminds him of the smoke from the burning truck.

He is not suicidal, he says, but he is tired. Tired of the hypervigilance, the flashbacks, the feeling that he is still trapped under that truck, listening to Elias die. He wants to feel like himself again, but he does not know who that man is anymore. He looks at his hands, once used to steer a truck through danger, and sees only the hands that failed to save a friend.
